Atlanta (/ætˈlæn(t)ə/) is the capital of the U.S. state of Georgia.
Atlanta is the seat of Fulton County, and a portion extends into neighboring DeKalb County.
The population of Atlanta within city limits was 510,823 according to the 2020 U.S. census.
Atlanta is the eighth most populous city in the Southeast and 37th most populous city in the United States.
Atlanta is the principal city of a larger metropolitan area including Cobb, Clayton, and Gwinnett counties, along with Fulton and DeKalb.
The Atlanta metropolitan area has more than 6.3 million people (2023 estimate).
Atlanta is situated among the foothills of the Appalachian Mountains at an elevation of just over 1,000 feet (300 m) above sea level.
Atlanta features unique topography that includes rolling hills, lush greenery, and dense urban tree coverage.
Atlanta was originally founded as a terminus for a major state-sponsored railroad.
It soon became a convergence point among several railroads, leading to rapid growth.
The largest was the Western and Atlantic Railroad, from which Atlanta's name is derived.
During the American Civil War, Atlanta served a strategically important role for the Confederacy until it was captured in 1864.
General William T. Sherman's March to the Sea almost entirely burned Atlanta to the ground.
Atlanta rebounded dramatically after the war and quickly became an industrial center and unofficial capital of the "New South".
After World War II, Atlanta also became a manufacturing and technology hub.
During the 1950s and 1960s, it became a major organizing center for the American civil rights movement.
Martin Luther King Jr., Ralph Abernathy, and many other locals played prominent roles in the movement's leadership.
In the modern era, Atlanta has remained a major transportation hub with Hartsfield-Jackson International Airport becoming the world's busiest airport by passenger traffic since 1998.
Atlanta has an economy with a nominal GDP of $473 billion as of 2021.

Its economy is considered diverse, including sectors such as transportation, aerospace, logistics, healthcare, news and media operations, film and television production, information technology, finance, and biomedical research and public policy.
Atlanta hosted the 1996 Summer Olympics, impacting its development into the 21st century by significantly investing in universities, parks, and tourism.
The gentrification of some neighborhoods has intensified since the 2000s with the growth of the Atlanta Beltline.
This has altered demographics, politics, aesthetics, and culture.
Atlanta's Piedmont Park received a winter snowfall under 4 inches (10 cm) in January 2023.
The population density was 3,685.45 persons per square mile (1,422.95/km²) as of the 2020 census.
Atlanta's racial and ethnic makeup includes 51.0% Black or African American, 40.9% non-Hispanic white, 4.2% Asian, and 0.3% Native American.
4% of the population reported two or more races.
0% of the city's population were Hispanic or Latino.
The median income for a household in Atlanta was $77,655 as of 2022.
The per capita income for the city was $60,778 as of 2022.
Approximately 17.7% percent of the population was living below the poverty line as of 2022.
In 2024, 391,711 residents lived in Fulton County and 28,292 lived in DeKalb County.
The Black population began to grow significantly in Southern metropolitan cities like Atlanta after the New Great Migration from California and the North.
Atlanta has long been known as a center of African-American political power, education, entrepreneurship, and culture.
In the 1990s, Atlanta started experiencing Black flight with many moving to suburbs for lower costs or better public schools.
The city's share of Black residents shrank from 67% in 1990 to 47% in 2020.
Blacks made up nine percent of new Atlanta residents between 2010 and 2020.
Atlanta is home to a sizable foreign-born Black population, notably from Eritrea, Ethiopia, Ghana, Somalia, Liberia, and Nigeria.
The non-Hispanic white population began rebounding after decades of white flight to suburbs.
Between 2000 and 2020, the proportion of whites in the city grew strongly.
In two decades, Atlanta's White population grew from 33% to 39% of the city's population.
Whites made up the majority of new residents between 2010 and 2020.
The Hispanic and Latino populations have grown significantly in recent years.
The largest Hispanic ancestries are Mexican, Puerto Rican, and Cuban.
There is a growing population along Buford Highway and I-85 corridor.
Metro Atlanta had the 19th largest Hispanic population in the United States in 2013.
Atlanta has a thriving and diverse LGBT community with 12.8% of the city's total population identifying as LGB according to a survey by the Williams Institute.
Midtown and Cheshire Bridge areas have historically been the epicenters of LGBT culture.
Atlanta formed a reputation for being inclusive after former mayor Ivan Allen Jr. dubbed it "the city too busy to hate" in the 1960s.
Atlanta has consistently scored 100% on the Human Rights Campaign's Municipal Equality Index.
Religion in Atlanta is now more diverse, with 73% of residents identifying as some type of Christian according to the Public Religion Research Institute in 2020.
Historically centered on Protestant Christianity, it now includes Roman Catholic and ethnic or national churches like Korean and Indian congregations.
The larger non-Christian faiths are Judaism, Islam, and Hinduism.
Atlanta's economy is the 8th-largest in the country and the 15th-largest in the world with a GDP of $385 billion.
Corporate operations play a major role as Atlanta claims the nation's third-largest concentration of Fortune 500 companies (tied for third with Chicago).
It hosts global headquarters of several corporations such as The Coca-Cola Company, The Home Depot, Delta Air Lines, and others.
Over 75% of Fortune 1000 companies conduct business operations in the city's metro area.
The region hosts offices of over 1,250 multinational corporations.
Atlanta was born as a railroad town with logistics continuing to represent an important part of its economy.
In 2021, Norfolk Southern moved their headquarters to Atlanta.
Hartsfield–Jackson Atlanta International Airport is the world's busiest airport and Delta Air Lines' global hub.
UPS operates an air cargo hub at Hartsfield-Jackson.
Media is also an important aspect with media mogul Ted Turner founding CNN in the city.
Cox Enterprises moved its headquarters to Atlanta, now the nation's third-largest cable television service.
Notable sports networks headquartered in Atlanta include Warner Bros. Discovery Sports, NBA TV, Bally Sports South, and Bally Sports Southeast.
The Weather Channel is based just outside of the city in suburban Cobb County.
Information technology has become increasingly important with Atlanta earning the nickname "Silicon peach".
As of 2013, it contains the fourth-largest concentration of IT jobs in the US, numbering 85,000+.
Atlanta is also ranked as the sixth fastest-growing for IT jobs.
Recently, Atlanta has been the center for film and television production due to the Georgia Entertainment Industry Investment Act.
Film and television production facilities include Techwood Studios, Pinewood Atlanta Studios, Tyler Perry Studios, Williams Street Productions, and EUE/Screen Gems soundstages.
Film and television production injected $9.5 billion into Georgia's economy in 2017.
Atlanta has emerged as the all-time most popular destination for film production in the United States and one of the top ten globally.
Compared to other American cities, Atlanta's economy was disproportionately affected by the Great Recession.
From 2010 to 2011, it saw a 0.9% contraction in employment and plateauing income growth at 0.4%.
Unemployment had decreased to 7% by late 2014 but was still higher than the national unemployment rate of 5.8%.
Atlanta's housing market struggled with home prices dropping by 2.1% in January 2012 and reaching levels not seen since 1996.
The average home price plummeted to 17.3% in February 2012, the largest annual drop in history for any American or global city.
Despite these challenges, Atlanta's real estate market has resurged since 2012 with median home value and rent growth significantly outpacing the national average by 2018.
Atlanta is one of few U.S. cities with permanent, professional, and resident companies in all major performing arts disciplines: opera, ballet, orchestral music, and theater.
The Atlanta Opera, Atlanta Ballet, Atlanta Symphony Orchestra, and Alliance Theatre are based there.
Atlanta attracts many touring Broadway acts, concerts, shows, and exhibitions catering to a variety of interests.
The Woodruff Arts Center is home to the Atlanta Symphony Orchestra and the Alliance Theatre.
The High Museum of Art is arguably the South's leading art museum.
The Museum of Design Atlanta (MODA) and SCAD FASH Museum of Fashion + Film are the only such museums in the Southeast.
Contemporary art museums include the Atlanta Contemporary Art Center and the Museum of Contemporary Art of Georgia.
Emory University's Michael C. Carlos Museum contains the largest collection of ancient art in the Southeast.
The Spelman College Museum of Fine Art is the only museum to focus on art by women of the African diaspora.
Georgia Tech's Robert C. Williams Paper Museum features the largest collection of paper and paper-related artifacts in the world.
Atlanta has become one of the U.S.'s best cities for street art, hosting Living Walls and the Outerspace Project.
Examples of street art can be found on the Atlanta Street Art Map.
Atlanta emerged as a center for country music in the 1920s brought by migrants from Appalachia.
During the countercultural 1960s, it hosted the Atlanta International Pop Festival.
The city was also a center for Southern rock during its heyday with bands like the Allman Brothers Band and Lynyrd Skynyrd performing there.
In the 1980s, Atlanta had an active punk rock scene centered on venues like the 688 Club and Metroplex.
Atlanta hosted the Sex Pistols' first U.S. show at the Great Southeastern Music Hall in 1979.
The city produced major mainstream acts across many genres including Travis Tritt, Xscape, TLC, Usher, and Toni Braxton.
Atlanta gave birth to Atlanta hip hop with artists like Outkast and Dungeon Family gaining relevance and success.
In the 2000s, Atlanta moved from the margins to become hip-hop's center of gravity with sub-genres like crunk.
The city was recognized by Vice magazine for its indie rock scene revolving around venues on the alternative eastside.
The state government provides qualified businesses and productions a 15% transferable income tax credit for in-state costs of music investments.
Atlanta is home to Tyler Perry Studios, one of the largest film production studios in the U.S.
It doubles for other parts of the world and fictional settlements in blockbuster productions like The Fast and the Furious franchise and Marvel features.

Notable films set in Atlanta include Gone With the Wind (1939), Smokey and the Bandit (1977), The Dukes of Hazzard (1979), Sharky's Machine (1981), The Slugger's Wife (1985), Driving Miss Daisy (1989), ATL (2006), Ride Along (2014), and Baby Driver (2017).

The city provides the backdrop for shows like Ozark, Watchmen, The Walking Dead, Stranger Things, Love Is Blind, Star, Dolly Parton's Heartstrings, The Outsider, The Vampire Diaries, The Real Housewives of Atlanta, Love & Hip Hop: Atlanta, and Atlanta.
Atlanta has a festival season stretching from January through November with over 100 festivals annually.

Some notable festivals include the Atlanta Dogwood Festival, Shaky Knees Music Festival, Dragon Con, Peachtree Road Race, Music Midtown, Atlanta Film Festival, National Black Arts Festival, Festival Peachtree Latino, Atlanta Pride, and neighborhood festivals in Inman Park, Atkins Park, Virginia-Highland (Summerfest), and Little Five Points Halloween.
Atlanta is the seventh-most visited city in the United States with over 35 million visitors per year.
The Georgia Aquarium is the most popular attraction among visitors.

Other major attractions include historical museums like Martin Luther King Jr. National Historical Park, Atlanta Cyclorama & Civil War Museum, World of Coca-Cola, College Football Hall of Fame, and National Center for Civil and Human Rights.
Outdoor attractions like Atlanta Botanical Garden, Zoo Atlanta, and festivals showcase arts and crafts, film, and music.
Atlanta's culinary scene includes a mix of urban establishments, ethnic restaurants, and traditional Southern dining.

Since the turn of the 21st century, it has emerged as a sophisticated restaurant town with notable establishments like Bocado, Bacchanalia, Miller Union, Empire State South, Two Urban Licks, and Rathbun's.
Atlanta is home to professional franchises for four major team sports: Atlanta Braves (MLB), Atlanta Hawks (NBA), Atlanta Falcons (NFL), and Atlanta United FC (MLS).
The city regularly hosts international, professional, and collegiate sporting events like the Super Bowl, PGA Tour events, NCAA Final Four Men's Basketball Championship, and College Football Playoff.
Atlanta is known as the "capital" of college football in America with four-time national champion Georgia Tech Yellow Jackets and Georgia State Panthers.
It is within a few hours driving distance of many SEC universities hosting annual events like Aflac Kickoff Game, Celebration Bowl, MEAC/SWAC Challenge, and Chick-fil-A Peach Bowl.
Atlanta hosted the 1996 Summer Olympics and will host the 2026 FIFA World Cup.
The city hosts the Atlanta Open men's professional tennis tournament every summer.
Running is popular with the Peachtree Road Race being the world's largest 10 km race annually on Independence Day.
The Atlanta Marathon routes through historic landmarks starting and ending at Centennial Olympic Park.
Atlanta has a network of freeways radiating from the city, making automobiles the dominant means of transportation.
Three major interstates converge in Atlanta: I-20 (east-west), I-75 (northwest-southeast), and I-85 (northeast-southwest).
The Downtown Connector (I-75/85) is one of the most congested segments, carrying over 340,000 vehicles daily.
Atlanta is mostly encircled by Interstate 285, known as "the Perimeter," marking the boundary between Inside and Outside the Perimeter.
The Metropolitan Atlanta Rapid Transit Authority (MARTA) provides public transportation with buses, heavy rail, and a downtown light rail loop.
Despite heavy automotive usage, MARTA's subway system is the eighth busiest in the country.
Hartsfield–Jackson Atlanta International Airport is the world's busiest airport by passenger traffic since 1998.
The airport offers air service to over 150 U.S. destinations and more than 75 international destinations in 50 countries, with over 2,500 daily arrivals and departures.
Atlanta has a growing cycling culture with the first "bike track" constructed on 10th Street in Midtown.
The city received a bike sharing program called Relay Bike Share starting in June 2016.
According to the 2016 American Community Survey, 68.6% of working Atlanta residents commuted by driving alone, 7% carpooled, 10% used public transportation, and 4.6% walked.
About 2.1% used other forms like taxis, bicycles, and motorcycles.
Atlanta declared itself a "welcoming city" in January 2017 but does not consider itself a sanctuary city.
The Atlanta Police Department numbers around 2,000 officers and has seen a 40% decrease in the city's crime rate between 2001 and 2009.
In 2023, it was estimated that about 1,000 gangs were responsible for at least 70% of all crime including identity theft, credit card fraud, and human trafficking.
The Atlanta Fire Rescue Department provides fire protection and first responder emergency medical services from its 35 fire stations.
In 2017, AFRD responded to over 100,000 calls for service covering 135.7 square miles.
Atlanta has a tree canopy coverage of 47.9% as of 2017, the highest among all major American cities.
Trees Atlanta, founded in 1985, has planted and distributed over 113,000 shade trees in the city.
The city government has awarded $130,000 in grants to neighborhood groups for tree planting.
Fees are imposed on developers that remove trees per a citywide ordinance active since 1993.
